places.name: Vũ Linh Đường
places.size: A minor sect of bell casters: about 45 casters, hangers and wall-keepers, a walled compound about 300 m across with about 35 buildings and a tall bell frame; young (founded 930).
places.where: Grassland at 270 m, inland, on the grass above Thu Trì Thành. Wood qi. Neutral vassal of Thính Vũ Lâu. Nearest: the village Tượng Lộ 141 km, the spirit vein Trúc Căn Huyệt 236 km. Map crop: a bright green grassland clearing among dark forest pockets, with no water in view: inland, rolling and gentle, thin rivulets at the lower edges.
places.imagined: A rainy dusk: bells of every size hanging in the open, each ringing a different note under the rain.
places.subject: The place: Vũ Linh Đường, the Hall of Rain Bells, a small sect of bell casters, seen from above rainy grassland. Setting: green rolling grassland on a rise above a distant river town, low grey cloud, light steady rain, silver puddles on the paths. The compound is a walled yard about three hundred metres across with a grey-tile wall, one gate tower, and about thirty-five buildings: a long casting shed with a smoking chimney and a round furnace yard where bronze is poured, clay mould sheds, a main hall with a curved roof, dormitories, a tuning house, and storerooms of bronze ingots. Its signature is the bell frame: a tall timber gantry tower with three tiers of crossbeams, hung with more than a hundred bells of every size, from hand-bells to temple bells taller than a man, in rows, each streaming with rain and each ringing a different soft note; along the compound wall hang more bells under a long roofed gallery, and the wall-keepers walk it with tuning mallets. Great unfinished bells stand on trestles in the yard, with two sit on the ground, green with fresh patina. About forty figures in dark rain-cloaks are at work, tiny. Soft grey-silver light from the upper left, gleam on wet roofs, long dim shadows. Nine of the largest bells are cast in a row of pits in the yard, and the casting shed's roof is raised on posts so that smoke escapes. A tuning house with open walls holds a set of twenty-four bells on a single frame, played with long padded beams by two disciples at once. The wall-keepers' path runs along the top of the compound wall for its whole length, hung with bells at each post, and at its gate a keeper checks every note of a traveller's bell against a reed pipe. Heaps of broken bell-metal lie sorted by colour for recasting.

places.name: Xuyên Lâm Môn
places.size: A minor sect of staff fighters and forest guides: about 60 members and twice as many hired porters, a gate and a stair with small halls on narrow terraces, about 45 buildings along a ridge about 800 m long.
places.where: High mountain at 1.14 km, on a shoulder of Kinh Trập Sơn above the rain forest, the pass where the forest road leaves the thunder ridge. Metal qi. A righteous sect under a ma đạo lord. Nearest: the ruin Thủ Lôi Bảo 100 km, the peak Thần Cổ Phong 146 km. Map crop: bare grey crags with snow on the highest peaks, forest pockets in the southern valleys, a thin river at the lower right and open grassland to the south-east; no sea in view.
places.imagined: Morning, rain beating the leaves below, a traveller handed a worn hardwood staff.
places.subject: The place: Xuyên Lâm Môn, the Gate Through the Forest, a sect of staff guides, seen from above a high mountain shoulder in rain. Setting: a high bare shoulder of Kinh Trập Sơn among grey and snow-capped crags, with dark rain forest filling the valleys to the south and running to the horizon in many greens under mist, a pale road leaving the thunder ridge. At the head of a long stair that drops straight down into the trees stands a sect gate of plain grey stone, two pillars with a lintel and a tiled roof. Beside it an open-sided gatehouse holds long racks of worn hardwood guide staffs, hundreds of them, in lines. A traveller with a bundle and a mule, tiny, receives one staff; a long line of hired porters with loads waits on the stair. Above the gate, small halls of grey stone and dark timber climb the ridge on narrow terraces, about forty-five buildings: a main hall with grey roof, practice yards of beaten earth where staff fighters spar in pairs, dormitories, a hostel, stables, store sheds for rope and rice, and a bell tower. Narrow paths wind into the forest from the stair's foot. A small guide party sets out downward in file. Rain falling, silver light from the upper left, wet stone, long soft shadows. The stair has four hundred and eight steps, with a landing and a tea-shed every hundred, and a rope rail along its whole length. Beyond the gate-house stands a drilling floor of grey flagstones sixty metres square, scarred by generations of staff-ends. The guides' hall has a long veranda carved with the names of the first forty chiefs, and in the stables sixty mules stand under a straw roof. Porters' sleeping sheds hold two hundred hired porters in tiered bunks, and a tally-hut records every staff given and returned.

places.name: Không Mông Thành
places.size: A walled port city in a valley mouth: about 2.8 km across, some 22,000 roofs and about 100,000 people, with every street roofed by covered arcades.
places.where: Grassland at -40 m, coast and river, a low valley mouth by the sea. Water qi. Holder Thính Vũ Lâu; founded by Khải Lôi Môn in 200. Nearest: the spirit vein Vi Vũ Tuyền 127 km. Map crop: a straight west coast with a great blue sea to the west, a river entering the sea at the city's edge, patchwork terraced fields to the south, forest in between, and bare grey mountains to the north-east.
places.imagined: Fine hazy rain: arcades of grey tile on red-painted posts, drums beating under them for the first thunder.
places.subject: The place: Không Mông Thành, Hazy Rain City, seen from above through a fine hazy rain. Setting: a low valley opening to a grey sea, green forested hills and, farther back, bare grey mountains soft in mist, a river entering the bay, low cloud and pale veils of rain. The city is a walled port about two and eight-tenths kilometres across, a grey stone wall with ten gate towers, enclosing about twenty-two thousand grey-tile roofs in dense blocks. Every street is roofed by long covered arcades of grey tile on red-painted posts, so from above the city looks like a network of long grey double-pitched ridges with red lines of posts below, hundreds of straight roof-lines running down the valley to the harbour. Above the arcades rise the older halls of the Thunder Gate's age, with roof ridges capped in green bronze that gleams wet, and a bronze-roofed drum tower at the centre. A broad harbour basin holds sixty ships under rain. In a central square, hundreds of people beat drums under the arcades in a thunder-day festival, tiny figures in rain capes, with colourful umbrellas and lanterns. Canals reflect the red posts. Dim silver light from the upper left through haze. Around the city lie small rice terraces and tea slopes; across the river a long causeway leads to a lighthouse on a rock. The arcades are two storeys on the main avenues, with shops below and families above, and the posts are painted a red so deep it looks wet. The central drum tower stands forty metres tall, its eaves curled and green with bronze; every first thunder a hundred drummers beat it. Rain-barrels of stone stand at every junction, and umbrellas are sold in the arcades at every post.

places.name: Hạnh Hoa Thị
places.size: A market town of about 900 houses and stalls and 4,000 people in deep narrow lanes along a river, about 900 m long.
places.where: Steppe at 70 m on a river below the southern road to Thính Vũ Lâu. Earth qi. Holder Thính Vũ Lâu. Nearest: the mine Hắc Tích Khoáng 103 km, the ruin Hạ Lôi Thành 112 km. The poem of spring rain and apricot blossom for sale. Map crop: a river basin of grass among bare rugged mountains with orange ridges in the north, a black volcanic cone about a hundred kilometres to the south-west, and a river looping round it; no sea in view.
places.imagined: The morning after spring rain: lanes roofed in pink and white by baskets of apricot blossom hung from every eave.
places.subject: The place: Hạnh Hoa Thị, Apricot Blossom Market, seen from above the morning after spring rain. Setting: a grassy basin among bare crags with a river curving along one side and thin apricot trees crowding the river bank, in full pink-white bloom, with the road to the dark volcanic hills winding off to the north. The market is built of deep narrow lanes, about thirty of them, between tall grey-tile houses with steep roofs packed shoulder to shoulder, with a crooked main lane following the river and a market square at the bend. From every eave hangs a woven basket of apricot blossom, thousands of them, so that after the rain the lanes are roofed in pink and white, the grey roofs almost hidden under strings of baskets and fallen petals. Stalls selling flowers, tea, and cakes line the lanes; at one corner a healer's house with a white sign-less awning has a queue of sick people waiting among the buyers. Buyers with baskets and umbrellas, porters, a girl with flowers, tiny figures; a few boats at the landing. Petals drift on the water. Soft pearly light from the upper left, fine mist, long faint shadows to the lower right. The lanes are numbered on lintels carved with a single apricot flower, and at the market's centre stands a small square with a drum and a well. Eight flower-sellers' stalls are stacked with baskets in pyramids, and pickers sit along the river wall tying blossom sprays into bundles. Behind the market, apricot orchards cover the river bank in a pink cloud for two kilometres; the healer's house at the east end has an open courtyard with a long bench of waiting patients under a canopy of baskets.

places.name: Lãng Hoa Thành
places.size: A walled port city on a steppe coast: about 2.4 km across, some 15,000 roofs and about 65,000 people, with a sea wall about 2 km long pierced by hundreds of blowholes.
places.where: Dry, wind-bitten steppe at sea level on the coast at a river mouth. Water qi. Holder Thính Vũ Lâu, founded 800 after the Pirate Purge. Nearest: the spirit vein Hải Khí Nhãn 103 km. Map crop: a river mouth on the north shore of a big blue bay, bare grey mountains to the north-east, thick dark forest to the south-west, and grassy hills between; the coast faces open water to the south-east.
places.imagined: A storm day: white spray bursting from the stone blowholes in plumes like flowers along the whole waterfront.
places.subject: The place: Lãng Hoa Thành, Wave Flower City, seen from above on a stormy day. Setting: a wind-bitten coast of pale grass hills bending in the wind, dark forest to the south-west and bare grey mountains at the north-east, a heavy grey-green sea throwing big waves onto a straight coast, a river mouth with a harbour on one side. The city is walled on the land side and shielded by a sea wall of grey stone about two kilometres long, pierced with rows of carved stone blowholes, hundreds of them in lines, and when the waves strike the wall white spray bursts from every one in tall plumes like flowers all along the waterfront, a long garland of white against the grey. Behind the wall, about fifteen thousand grey-tile roofs climb a low rise in terraces toward a watch hall on its summit, with a tall stone watchtower, with salt-boiling yards in smoking rows, drying racks of fish, fishing boats pulled up on a protected slipway, and a small harbour in the river mouth with thirty boats. Along the top of the wall, dozens of children run racing the spray, tiny figures, while one is drenched by the biggest plume. Salt-boilers' chimneys smoke in the wind, which blows the smoke flat. Light from the upper left, sharp and cold, long shadows to the lower right. The blowholes are carved as lotus and lion heads, each a metre wide, and spaced every three or four paces along the wall; when a big wave strikes, a hundred plumes stand up together in a ripple. Salt-boiling yards, twenty of them, stand along the south side with chimneys of clay and long drying beds. The watch hall's tower carries a signal mast, and its steps are lined with bronze bells. In the river mouth the fishing fleet of sixty small boats rocks inside a stone mole, and a long line of salt-carts waits at the east gate.

places.name: Vọng Hải Trấn
places.size: A walled coastal town of about 1,000 roofs and 4,500 people at a river mouth, with a line of about 12 watchtowers along sea cliffs about 3 km long.
places.where: Bamboo forest at sea level on the coast at a river mouth, below low sea cliffs. Wood qi. Held by Xuyên Lâm Môn. Nearest: the beast lair Lân Giáp Cốc 79 km. Map crop: a river mouth on the west shore of a great blue bay, rolling golden-green grass hills inland with bamboo and forest pockets, a larger forest to the south-west; the coast is gentle with a few rocks.
places.imagined: Dawn. Tall watchtowers with bamboo upper storeys, each with a signal frame looking out over the gulf.
places.subject: The place: Vọng Hải Trấn, Sea-Watching Town, seen from above a coastal bamboo forest at dawn. Setting: a low line of sea cliffs of pale grey rock about three kilometres long, a great calm bay of silver-blue beyond, rolling golden-green hills inland, thick coastal bamboo in feathery green along the cliff top, and a river mouth cutting the cliff in a gap. The town stands in the gap, a walled place about seven hundred metres across with a grey-brick wall, a sea gate with a quay, about a thousand grey-tile roofs in tight lanes, a fish market, a small harbour with thirty boats, a bamboo-framed granary and a shrine. Along the cliff tops stand about twelve watchtowers spaced a few hundred metres apart, each looking out over the gulf. Watchers in dark jackets stand on the towers, tiny figures; the nearest tower is manned by two figures with a spyglass. A watch bell hangs at the town gate. Soft pink dawn light from the upper left, long shadows, mist on the water. The towers are grey stone to about ten metres, then bamboo for another eight, each with a platform, a roof and a signal frame of poles hung with coloured cloths, and a path of pale gravel links them along the cliff edge. The town's wall is of packed earth with a bamboo palisade, and the sea-gate has a heavy beam that is slid across at night. Boats of two kinds use the quay: slender watch-boats painted in stripes, and broad fishing boats. In the square a sentry roster is posted on twelve boards, one for each tower, and a watcher caught asleep carries water in two buckets along the lanes.

places.name: Phong Đăng Trấn
places.size: A walled harbour town of about 1,300 roofs and 6,000 people with a great steelyard balance in the main gate.
places.where: Fertile river meadows at sea level on the coast. Wood qi. Holder Thính Vũ Lâu. Nearest: the lightning wood Lôi Trúc Lâm 125 km. The Lục family's harvests, the first grain tax collected here. Map crop: a river mouth on the north shore of a bay, hilly gold-green farmland with dark forest pockets and a river along the left edge; another small bay shows at the top.
places.imagined: The first cart of the harvest tax weighed on the great steelyard, the whole town watching the beam.
places.subject: The place: Phong Đăng Trấn, Abundant Harvest Town, seen from above fertile river meadows by the sea at harvest. Setting: green and gold fields heavy with grain in neat squares and strips across a wide river plain, tree-lined canals and dykes, a river mouth to a grey-blue sea, with a little harbour. The town is walled, about eight hundred metres across, with a grey-brick wall and four gates, about thirteen hundred grey-tile roofs, a harbour on the river side with forty boats, and granaries with thatched roofs. In the main gate, which is a double-storey gatehouse, hangs a huge wooden steelyard balance, its beam as long as a boat, hung from a gate-beam on a rope chain, with a great iron weight and a platform on which a loaded grain cart is weighed for the tax before it enters. Long lines of grain carts queue on the road outside, hundreds of them, in a line a kilometre long across the fields, piled with sacks, with oxen. The first cart is on the beam, with the whole town gathered, a tiny crowd around the gate and on the wall, and tax clerks with abacuses. Golden light from the upper left, long shadows, dust in the air. Its fields are laid in long thin strips, each ploughed in a different direction by the family that works it, so that the plain looks like woven cloth. The steelyard's beam is of ironwood, six metres long, hung from the gate arch on three chains, with a sliding weight of cast iron the size of a barrel; a clerk with a brass ruler reads the beam. Beside the gate, a tax house with a green roof holds the ledgers. A line of eighty carts stands ready, and each carter holds a scoop of his best grain.

places.name: Ương Ca Thôn
places.size: A hill village of about 35 houses and 150 people at the top of about 40 curving rice terraces, with one round stone stage.
places.where: Grassland hills at 280 m above a river. Wood qi. Holder Thính Vũ Lâu. Nearest: the lightning wood Tiêu Đồng Lâm 79 km, the village Ô Diêu 175 km. Map crop: a river valley with a stair of paddy terraces to the west, dark forest hills to the east, bare grey crags to the north and a bay of the sea at the top-left; the village stands on the east side of the river.
places.imagined: Planting day, singers on the round stone stage.
places.subject: The place: Ương Ca Thôn, Planting Song Village, seen from above a hillside at planting time. Setting: green hills rolling to a misty horizon, a river in the valley below, light cloud. A stair of about forty curving rice terraces descends the hillside in sweeping contour lines, each terrace a thin ribbon of water that mirrors the sky, with green seedlings planted in the lower ones and dark flooded earth above, the whole slope like a great shell. At the top stand about thirty-five grey-tile houses in a tight cluster with yards, a threshing floor, water buffalo sheds, and a small shrine. At the head of the terraces stands a round stone stage about twenty metres across, open to the sky, ringed by low stone benches, where a line of singers stands at planting, in bright blue and white clothes, tiny figures, while below them the whole village, about a hundred people, plants the terraces in long rows to the song. A thin stone-paved path winds down along the terrace walls to the river. Light from the upper left, long shadows across the terraces, reflected in the water. The terraces are cut about forty paces wide, with stone retaining walls capped by earthen bunds, and the planting rows follow the contour exactly. A narrow stair of flat stones runs straight down the middle from the stage to the river. The stage has a ring of twelve low stone pillars, one for each month, and a flat dais in the centre; on planting morning the singers wear blue and white, and the planters answer from the terraces below, line by line. A stone gong hangs on a frame at the rim and is struck three times to begin.

places.name: Song Khê Thôn
places.size: A village of about 30 houses and 130 people where two brooks join in a Y, with one tiny roofed shrine.
places.where: Grassland at 40 m on a river. Wood qi. Holder Thính Vũ Lâu. Nearest: the beast lair Hoàng Phong Cốc 90 km, the lightning wood Kiếp Trúc Lâm 90 km. Map crop: dense forest hills in the north-west and a green valley with a river running down to a large blue gulf on the east; the village sits where two streams meet above the bay.
places.imagined: A couple drinking from both brooks with the joined dippers.
places.subject: The place: Song Khê Thôn, Twin Brooks Village, seen from above a green valley. Setting: a soft green grassland valley with dark forest on the hills, two brooks winding down from opposite sides: one clear and silver-blue, one tea-brown from the forest peat, flowing side by side after they meet in a Y shape, the two colours running in two stripes for a long way before mixing. Below the Y, on the grassy banks among cranes standing in the clear brook, stand about thirty grey-tile houses with small yards, willows, a plank bridge over each brook, a mill by the clear stream, a dye house by the brown one, and vegetable plots. On the point of land where the brooks meet stands a tiny roofed shrine, hardly bigger than a cupboard, with a red-lacquered roof, and two bamboo dippers tied together by a red cord. A young couple kneels at the point drinking from both brooks with the joined dippers, tiny figures; behind them three more couples wait, a matchmaker with a long red cord, and visitors who have come from far. Light from the upper left, soft long shadows, mist rising from the water. The clear brook runs over a bed of white pebbles, and the brown one over dark leaf-mould, so the two lie side by side in the pool below the shrine like two ribbons for nearly a hundred metres. The red cord is a hand-plaited silk rope, a metre long, bleached by years of sun. A stone bench by the shrine seats four, and the village bridges are of single flat stones. The matchmaker's house, with a lantern, stands nearest the point, and a line of couples waits on the path, each carrying a gift of two red eggs.

places.name: Thượng Độ Thôn
places.size: A ferry village of about 30 houses and 130 people with a rope ferry between two tall carved stone posts.
places.where: Grassland at 150 m on the upper river. Wood qi. Holder Thính Vũ Lâu. Nearest: the forest Địch Trúc Lâm 75 km. Reached by Phượng Minh raiders in 1045. Map crop: a river valley of golden grassland and forest hills, a braided river running north to south, a second smaller river joining from the south-west; the ferry is on the east bank.
places.imagined: A ferry hauled across on a rope; the near stone post charred black to its top.
places.subject: The place: Thượng Độ Thôn, Upper Crossing Village, seen from above a river. Setting: a swift clear river about two hundred metres wide in a green upland valley with bamboo groves along its banks, hills behind with mist. Across the river is strung a thick rope, hauled tight between two tall carved stone posts, one on each bank, each about eight metres tall, carved with spirals. A broad ferry boat is hauled across on the rope by four ferrymen, carrying a cart, a mule, and a few passengers. The post on the near bank is charred black to its top, scorched in an old raid, and the villagers have never cleaned it; the far post is pale grey stone. On the near bank stand about thirty grey-tile houses with yards and a burnt-and-rebuilt landing of new pale timber beside old black stumps, a ferry-house, a tea shed, a few boats, and fish racks. A small group of grey-robed disciples stops by the black post, tiny figures looking up at it. A narrow road enters the bamboo. Light from the upper left, long shadows, thin mist over the river. The two posts are carved from a single grey stone each, with spirals and cloud-scrolls, and each bears an iron ring for the rope. The rope is as thick as a forearm, plaited from hemp, and runs in a long smooth curve across the water. The ferry has a flat deck twelve paces long, with a rail, and a bell at its prow. The charred post's black reaches thirteen paces up; at its foot an offering bowl holds a few copper coins. A small shrine with a red lintel stands on the bank, and a row of new bricks marks the rebuilt landing.

places.name: Hà Châu Thôn
places.size: A river village of about 40 houses and 170 people facing a raw new isle of mud and gravel about 300 m long.
places.where: Grassland at sea level on a river. Wood qi. Holder Thính Vũ Lâu, the isle claimed also by Xuyên Lâm Môn. Nearest: the lightning wood Hắc Đàn Mộc 79 km, the village Thượng Độ 168 km. Map crop: a braided river in a green-gold valley with dark forest pockets, the sea at the lower corners, and rolling grass hills; the isle sits in the river channel.
places.imagined: Morning, villagers rowing out to see whose boundary flag has been moved.
places.subject: The place: Hà Châu Thôn, River Isle Village, seen from above a broad river. Setting: a wide brown-green river about five hundred metres wide in a flat green lowland, willows and bamboo on the banks, and a pale morning sky. In the middle of the river lies a raw new isle of grey mud and gravel about three hundred metres long, raised out of the water in an earthquake: a bare pale lozenge with cracked mud, tilted slabs, seeps of water, and no plant on it. Two boundary flags of plain cloth, one red-black and one green, flap on poles at either end of the isle, which are blank, with a stone cairn at each. On the bank facing it stand about forty grey-tile houses along a lane, with a landing, fishing boats, drying nets, a ferry hut, and a small shrine. Eight small boats are rowed out from the village at once toward the isle, tiny figures in them, villagers going to check whose flag has moved, and two grey-robed officials stand on the isle itself measuring with ropes. Seabirds crowd the gravel. Light from the upper left, long shadows. The isle's mud has dried in a mosaic of cracked polygons, each a hand across, with a few shells and a drift of dead reeds along its edge. The two flags are of plain cloth on poles four metres high, each with a stone cairn at its foot, set exactly at the isle's ends. The village landing has eleven small boats, and a notice-board with two pegs where each side's claims are hung. Fishers cast nets from the isle's tail, and a dozen egrets stand on the gravel.

places.name: Kinh Điện Khoáng
places.size: A mine on a bare ridge about 3 km long, with about 12 open-air forges and pit mouths, about 40 buildings (smithies, sheds, barracks) and about 250 smiths and miners.
places.where: High mountain at 840 m on Kinh Trập Sơn. Metal qi. Holder Thính Vũ Lâu. Resource: fine iron (tinh thiết). Nearest: the mine Lôi Ngân Khoáng 75 km, the peak Dẫn Lôi Phong 79 km. Where storms strike the ore. Map crop: a bare grey and rust-orange mountain ridge, a small blue lake about a hundred kilometres to the south-east, a river in the top-right corner, and dark forest pockets to the north-west; no sea in view.
places.imagined: A storm. A tall iron rod above every forge catches lightning, the rock streaked with burn marks.
places.subject: The place: Kinh Điện Khoáng, the Lightning-Struck Mine, seen from above during a thunderstorm. Setting: a bare grey ridge of Kinh Trập Sơn, scored and streaked with black burn marks, dark thunderclouds piled over the ridge with a white lightning bolt hitting a rod in the middle distance, patchy green rain forest in the valleys below. Along the ridge stand about twelve open-air forges on bare rock beside the pit mouths: each a square stone hearth with a huge anvil block and a bellows, and above each a tall iron rod raised thirty metres, bristling like masts, to catch the lightning, with cables of braided wire running down into the forge. One forge is lit white-hot where a bolt has just hit, a stream of sparks flying out, and a smith in leather beside an enormous hammer, tiny. Pit mouths are black arches shored with dark timber, with ore carts on rails and heaps of rusty-brown ore and slag, and about forty buildings: slate-roofed smithies, ore sheds, a barracks, a store of hardwood clogs. Miners wear wooden shoes and carry no iron in the rain. Violet storm light from the upper left, glare of lightning, long shadows. Each forge is a stone enclosure about eight paces square with a low wall, and on its floor lies a great anvil of black iron, a trough of quenching water, and a rack of tongs. The lightning rods are of braided iron, thirty metres tall, bound with copper straps and set in stone footings, and the cables run to earth in pits lined with ore. The roofs of the smithies are of slate laid on iron rafters. Rain-slick wooden duckboards link the forges, and the miners' wooden shoes clatter on them. A watchman with a long bell stands on a pole platform to warn of strikes.

places.name: Tử Kim Khoáng
places.size: A mine on a steep slope: about 15 tunnel mouths in a cliff about 1 km wide, with long fans of purple spoil and about 30 buildings and 200 miners.
places.where: High mountain at 970 m, inland. Metal qi. Holder Thính Vũ Lâu. Resource: purple-gold sand (tử kim sa). Nearest: the ruin Hộ Khoáng Bảo 90 km, the peak Phi Lôi Phong 127 km. Map crop: a rugged grey mountain range with rust-orange ridges to the north, a bay of the sea at the lower-left about a hundred kilometres away, and a small lake to the north-east.
places.imagined: Before a storm: a seam glows faintly and miners leave the tunnels.
places.subject: The place: Tử Kim Khoáng, the Purple-Gold Mine, seen from above a steep mountain slope. Setting: a steep mountain face, grey-green forest below it and heavy dark purple storm clouds gathering in a sky of bruised violet with a break of gold light at one side. Fifteen tunnel mouths are set in a cliff about a kilometre wide, streaked purple and gold, in three rows of black arches with timber lintels, and from some a faint purple-gold glow shows inside. Below them long fans of purple-tinted spoil spill down the hillside in tongues, shining with gold flecks like glitter, with narrow ore-cart tracks zigzagging across the slope and a wooden sluice washing sand into settling pools that glitter amber and violet. About thirty buildings of grey stone with slate roofs: a smelter with a smoking chimney, ore stores, a barracks, a long sorting shed where purple-gold sand is picked, and a small shrine. Miners, about two hundred, come streaming out of the tunnels in a line with lamps, tiny figures, leaving before the storm. Light from the upper left on the spoil, deep shadows. The tunnels are in three tiers: four on the lowest, six on the middle and five above, each marked by a painted post. At the foot of each spoil fan stand wooden sluices where fine purple-gold sand is washed in shallow troughs, and the sluice-water runs a pale lavender. The smelter's chimney is of brick, fifteen metres tall, with a spiral of sparks at its crown. A sorting shed has benches along both sides, where boys pick shards with tweezers into small bowls. Mule-trains of twelve animals wind down the track every hour, each laden with two panniers.

places.name: Vũ Hoa Khoáng
places.size: A pebble-mine upland about 5 km across, a dozen long wooden sluices and about 40 buildings, with about 400 pickers; the richest ground of the sixteen.
places.where: High mountain at 1.87 km, a stony upland, inland. Metal qi. Holder Thính Vũ Lâu. Resource: spirit stone (linh thạch). Nearest: the peaks Hải Giác 79 km and Giảng Đạo 79 km. Rain-flower pebbles found in 500. Map crop: a high rugged grey range of bare ridges with rust-orange hills to the north, a bay of the sea about a hundred kilometres to the south-west, and a thin line of cloud over the peaks.
places.imagined: Rain on wet pebbles, whose colours show truest then; pickers sorting them.
places.subject: The place: Vũ Hoa Khoáng, the Rain-Flower Mine, seen from above in rain. Setting: the highest mine in the thunder mountains, a stony upland of grey rock and short wet grass about five kilometres across, with ridges of bare stone around it, cloud touching the peaks, and fine rain falling. The stream beds on the upland have been dammed into long wooden sluices, about a dozen, each two to three hundred metres long, stepping down the slope in a series of pale timber troughs with weirs and gates. In the sluices and in heaps beside them lie smooth pebbles of every colour: red, agate-banded, green, white, orange, violet, gleaming wet, so the troughs look like glittering ribbons of jewels, and the sorting tables beside them are piled in coloured mounds. About forty buildings of grey stone with slate roofs: pickers' sheds, long sorting halls with open sides, a counting house, a barracks and a small shrine. About four hundred pickers in rain capes crouch at the troughs and tables, tiny figures, sorting by colour into baskets. Soft grey light from the upper left, wet colours bright. The sluices carry a constant stream of rain-water, and every trough has a plank walkway beside it for the pickers. The pebbles are sorted into twelve colours in bins of woven bamboo, and the richest, the red agate-banded ones, are carried in lidded baskets to the counting house. The counting house has a weighing room with a brass balance and a steward's desk. A narrow stair of black stone leads up to a lookout pavilion with a view down the whole mine. Wet capes of straw hang from every post, and a gong rings when a rare stone is found.

places.name: Liệt Khuyết Phong
places.size: The highest summit of Kinh Trập Sơn at 4 km: a peak about 3 km across at its base, split by a rift about 800 m deep; no buildings, a few drill-yard stones for disciples.
places.where: High mountain at 4.0 km, inland. Metal qi. No holder. Nearest: the mine Lôi Tinh Khoáng 75 km, the ruin Nghênh Lôi Trại 79 km. The poet's line of lightning, thunder and crumbling ridges. Map crop: a jagged snow-streaked grey range of peaks and ridges with rust-orange hills at the upper-left, a few small lakes, and forest in a single patch to the north; no sea in view.
places.imagined: A storm: a sheer grey peak split from crown to shoulder as if by one stroke, rock fused black and glassy along the rift.
places.subject: The place: Liệt Khuyết Phong, the Peak of the Split Rift, seen from above in a thunderstorm. Setting: the highest summit of a great mountain range, a sheer grey peak rising above every other ridge, with storm clouds gathered thick on it, dark underneath and white-lit above, and a thin bolt of lightning striking the crown. The peak is split from crown to shoulder by a deep vertical rift, as if cut by one stroke, about eight hundred metres deep and fifty metres wide, with sheer straight walls, and the rock along the rift is fused black and glassy, shining like obsidian, in a seam running along both lips, and streaked with white scorch marks. Snow lies in the shadowed gullies of the upper slopes, and below the timber line dark forest runs down in a dark green skirt. On a high shoulder of bare rock a small drill yard of flat stones is marked with a few cairns, where a line of about twenty grey-robed disciples stands in the storm, tiny figures, drilling with swords raised toward the lightning. Down a narrow trail, a tiny bowl of rice is laid at intervals. Cold violet-white light, with gold from the upper left at the cloud edge, long dark shadows. The rift's lips are polished black glass, with white scorch rays running down the rock for a kilometre in all directions. Along the ridge to the east, a row of seven small cairns marks the places where disciples have drilled, each cairn made of stones brought up one by one. At the head of the trail a rain-hut of drystone stands with a roof of slate, and the rice bowls laid on the path are lined up like a row of white dots down the slope. Cloud pours into the rift like water into a well.
